html:
SMTO-POL-0013 — Permissions were changed somewhere else before you saved

GUID: baa9d5fd-6876-455e-8ee8-b1f0e41aa219
Slug: permission-revision-conflict
Domain: POL · Subsystem: pol

What happened

  • Someone else, or SMTO in another tab, changed these permission rules after you opened them. SMTO didn't save your edit, so that newer change wasn't erased.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Close any other SMTO tabs that are editing permissions, reload this page, and open the Permissions window again. Reloading shows the rules as they are saved now, including the other change.
  2. Under Apply to, pick the same place you were editing (This prompt, This conversation or Global) and see what changed. The other change might already do what you wanted, or you may want to keep it.
  3. Make only your intended change and select Apply. Saving on top of the latest rules keeps both your change and the other one.

What success looks like

  • Your change saves without an error, and reopening Permissions shows it alongside the other change.

If it still fails

  • If this keeps happening, someone else is saving at the same time; agree who edits, then try again. Otherwise select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't paste your old rules over the new ones without reading them first.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The permission-policy write was rejected because the stored revision for that scope is newer than the revision the editor loaded; another tab or client saved first.

What this means

  • Optimistic permission-policy revision checking detected a newer stored revision than the editor expected. Policy and approval decisions are scoped to their owning operation. Existing receipts determine prior effects; this explanation neither grants authority nor changes retry ownership.

Why this can happen

  • Optimistic permission-policy revision checking detected a newer stored revision than the editor expected.

How to diagnose it

  • Reload the current policy and compare its revision and changed rules with your intended edit.

How to fix it

  • Re-read the scope's policy and revision (PermissionAuthority.read_in / write_in in permission_scopes.py and memory_permission_scopes.py), merge the intended change with the current rules, and resubmit with the current expected revision. Do not resend the stale revision.
  • Reload the current permission policy, review the changed rules, and deliberately reapply only the intended scoped decision. Do not overwrite a newer policy blindly.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended edit is applied to the reviewed current revision without overwriting an unseen policy change.

What not to do

  • Do not submit a stale identifier or revision after another actor changed the resource.

Technical notes

  • Policy and approval decisions are scoped to their owning operation. Existing receipts determine prior effects; this explanation neither grants authority nor changes retry ownership.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
